post1.text:
Most companies don't stall at $50M because of a market problem. They stall because leadership didn't scale with the business.

Here's what that actually looks like in practice:

Stanford's Graduate School of Business recently highlighted that executives scaling AI across organizations often fail not because of the technology, but because of how they lead through uncertainty. The same principle applies to every major growth initiative.

Three things leaders at $50M+ businesses consistently get wrong:

1. They manage what got them here instead of building what gets them there. The skills and instincts that built a $50M company are often the ceiling of a $500M one.

2. They confuse delegation with abdication. Scaling requires letting go of decisions, not accountability.

3. They treat culture as a soft initiative. At scale, culture is an operational system. If it isn't intentionally built, it becomes a liability faster than any market shift will.

Leadership is the first constraint. Always.

What's the single leadership behavior you've had to unlearn as your company grew?

post2.text:
A recent piece in citybiz.co profiled Cyrille Bessière, an executive with a track record of scaling companies across industries. What stood out wasn't his resume. It was the pattern: every successful scaling effort required him to restructure how leadership communicated, decided, and prioritized before anything else changed.

At Autobahn Consultants, we see this constantly with companies pushing past $50M. The operational playbook gets rewritten at scale, but too many leaders try to execute new plays with old instincts.

Scaling isn't a strategy problem. It's a leadership alignment problem.

If your growth has plateaued or feels harder than it should, the bottleneck is almost never what you think it is.

Read the full article here and then ask yourself: is your leadership ready for the company you're building?

https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMipAFBVV95cUxNak50bU0tdnhPUUd3VElGLXhLcGNJRFpQcFhjMzdxWjFFYVk2Q0kwTWFybW4zQ29UWm1WY1NaeVJlakI4STJyZUxYWUpvdFlHZU1yenE0WjhKWTRXeXhKRVRFMVRnS0JkeU1teDlmTnltQWVMOERuaWVOOE5EM2JfbWRCajJYLUlIbnItMVRvLWxPX3ljNHY5SVFtSkp1OXRwaDc5Mg

post3.text:
When companies hire a new executive to accelerate growth, like YYForce recently did in appointing a Chief Strategic Officer, the announcement gets attention. But what happens in the 90 days after the hire? That's where scaling either takes hold or quietly falls apart.

Chapter 1 of Rock Your Business, titled Lead Like Lives Depend On It and written by Katherine Slain, confronts this directly. Katherine makes a case that leadership at scale is not an elevated version of what worked before. It's a fundamentally different job, and most leaders underestimate how fast that gap opens up.

One idea she surfaces early: the cost of a leadership identity that hasn't kept pace with company growth is not just personal. It's structural. It shows up in your org chart, your decisions, and your numbers.

The rest of the chapter builds from there in ways you won't expect.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Your exit is not a finish line. It is a mirror that reflects every decision you made while running your company.

Most founders spend years optimizing for revenue growth and almost no time optimizing for how that growth is valued by a buyer. That gap is expensive. A recent piece in Entrepreneur laid out exactly this problem: founders who delay exit planning until they are ready to sell consistently leave money on the table, because the conditions that drive a strong multiple take years to build, not months.

Three things $50M+ leaders should be doing right now:

1. Understand what drives your EBITDA multiple in your specific industry. Not all growth is valued equally by acquirers.

2. Reduce owner dependency before you need to. Buyers pay less for a business that cannot run without its founder.

3. Clean up your financials and your story. Buyers pay premiums for clarity, not potential.

The companies that exit well did not get lucky. They treated their exit as a strategic initiative years before they were ready to sell.

What would change about how you run your business today if you knew a buyer was evaluating it right now?

post2.text:
A recent piece from J.P. Morgan Private Bank breaks down the core exit strategy options available to business owners, from strategic sales to family succession to private equity recapitalizations.

The article is solid. But here is what it does not tell you: the strategy you choose matters far less than how prepared your business is when the moment arrives.

At Autobahn, we work with companies scaling from $50M to $500M and beyond. The ones who exit on their terms share one trait. They built their business as if a sophisticated buyer were watching from day one.

That means strong management teams, documented processes, diversified revenue, and financials that tell a clean story.

If you are in growth mode right now, your exit planning should already be in motion.

Read the J.P. Morgan piece here, then ask yourself whether your business is actually ready: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMitwFBVV95cUxOalJUT0c3NEFPTndZX08zeGN0dXVFOEJVcmVLRml0QUNjb2xXU3Nxd2ZjOW1mUVUtc0F6SDZ0M056b2Rpd21ZZWF6aVBpOHZESjRiMEtKYk13Sm52VTJJTzV5ZzhFVTE5LVVtcVN4aVpiUzJYUUEtclFONlM4S0NzS3owaFRDT3p6Z2NoZlhjSUh1QnhsWTkyT3pKQkJZR3YxWnZHSHpHTDQ3MEtSRDdBb1JDTVJrb1U?oc=5

post3.text:
A recent story in The American Bazaar followed a GovCon entrepreneur who scaled and exited successfully. The through line of his playbook was simple: he understood his valuation levers before he ever talked to a buyer.

That is exactly what Chapter 2 of our upcoming book addresses.

In "Rock Your Business: Navigating the Road from $50 Million to $500 Million and Beyond," chapter authors Paul Belair and George Hohman lay out exactly how scaling companies can maximize their multiple before going to market. The chapter title is "Maximize Your Multiple to Achieve Your Exit" and it does not start with the exit. It starts with the decisions you are making right now.

One thing Paul and George make clear: the multiple a buyer assigns to your business is not a negotiation. It is a conclusion they draw from years of evidence.

Are you building that evidence today?

Rock Your Business -- available soon. Follow us for updates.

The multiple a buyer assigns to your company is built over years, not negotiated in a deal room. post1.text:
Most leadership teams don't fail at strategy. They fail at deciding what to stop doing.

Forbes recently examined why execution breaks down at the leadership level, and the pattern is consistent: too many priorities, unclear ownership, and no honest accountability loop. Sound familiar?

Here is what scaling companies from $50M and beyond actually need to get right:

1. Strategy is not a planning event. It is a weekly operating discipline. If your leadership team only revisits the plan quarterly, you are already behind.

2. Accountability needs teeth. Not culture slogans. Someone owns each initiative, there is a measurable outcome, and the team reviews progress in real time.

3. The bottleneck is almost never the strategy document. It is the leadership team's willingness to have uncomfortable conversations when something is off track.

Companies that scale do not have better plans. They have better follow-through and a culture that treats execution as the strategy.

What is one thing your leadership team has agreed on but never truly held anyone accountable for?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Forbes breaks down exactly why leadership teams struggle to turn strategy into results. The core finding is not surprising to us: the gap between planning and execution is not a tools problem. It is a behavior problem.

At Autobahn Consultants, we see this constantly with companies in the $50M to $500M range. Leadership alignment looks strong in the boardroom and falls apart in the field. The strategy is clear on paper. The operating rhythm to support it is not.

The fix is not a new framework. It is consistent leadership behavior, defined ownership, and the courage to call out drift early.

If your team is experiencing this gap right now, this article is worth fifteen minutes of your time.

https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiugFBVV95cUxOSXpNczJQdVBKTWlEV0dsby1FaEFGUVg5X1B3Zk9qUGI2bDJMSUxydGhRdURFUUdERXhBRmNzUndTVXhITTREMzMxdk9faE5rUldabk9ld2p2dHdfeXJjVEpMckJ6dFZNckFkTkk5ZmJ5MHRVSm5iSXo2WGlwc0NoeTBvcUYxTF9pbUNmaDB4LUdlNk9pMll0Y01BRTNVYzJObzRrV3pCN19scHYtdThYcHJVUVFYbjFMbkE

post3.text:
The conversation around why strategy execution fails is everywhere right now. Forbes, leadership conferences, board rooms. But most of the answers stay theoretical.

Chapter 3 of Rock Your Business, titled 'What We Learned Selling Fish Food and Nike Shoes,' goes somewhere different. Authors Rafa Loyo and Jim Randall draw on real operational experience across completely different industries to show what disciplined execution actually looks like when the stakes are high and the playbook is still being written.

One thing they make clear: the companies that scale are not the ones with the most sophisticated strategy. They are the ones that build simple, repeatable systems and actually use them every week without exception.

That distinction is sharper than it sounds. The chapter unpacks why.

articles.snippet: The surprising economics of B2B growth: The new survival threshold—and what it takes to thrive  mckinsey.com

post1.text:
Most companies at $50M and beyond do not have a sales strategy. They have a collection of habits that worked when they were smaller.

That distinction costs them more than they realize. McKinsey research on B2B growth economics makes this clear: companies that fail to build deliberate, scalable growth engines do not just grow slower, they fall behind a survival threshold that is rising every year. Staying flat is no longer neutral. It is a slow decline.

Here is what that means for leaders running a $50M+ business:

First, revenue activity and revenue strategy are not the same thing. Busy sales teams can mask a broken foundation for years.

Second, your sales motion that closed your first $50M will not close your next $450M. The buyers, the complexity, and the competition have all changed.

Third, without a defined strategy, every quarter is a donation to your more disciplined competitors.

The question is not whether your team is working hard. The question is whether they are working inside a system designed to scale.

What would change in your business if you treated your sales strategy with the same rigor as your financial planning?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Gartner caught our attention: AI time savings in sales will not translate into revenue growth unless chief sales officers actively intervene to redirect that saved time toward high-value activities.

That finding matters enormously for companies scaling past $50M.

Here is Autobahn's take: technology does not fix a broken sales strategy. It accelerates whatever system you already have. If your reps are spending reclaimed hours on low-priority accounts or unfocused prospecting, AI just lets them do that faster.

The leaders winning right now are the ones who define exactly where that time should go before they roll out the tools.

If your sales strategy is not directing the behavior, your calendar will. And the calendar rarely picks the highest-value work.

Read the full Gartner findings here: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiYEFVX3lxTE83YmJZYVNxUUtqV1lJanRha3hGWnFtdjJYSm5FWURzTUFrVm1uTDB2R1VRWklWVlM4cVhURDNTMVFxVmw0Ql9YZUZrdndhcC1JWFRZczVJRmxlR1REQmVvMg?oc=5

post3.text:
A recent piece from abasto.com made a pointed argument: B2B sales strategy now requires AI and personalization to survive. We agree the landscape has shifted. But there is a step most companies skip before any of that becomes useful.

Chapter 4 of Rock Your Business, titled Every Day Without a Real Sales Strategy is a Donation, tackles this head on. Written by Deb and Brandon, the chapter draws a hard line between sales activity and sales strategy, and explains why companies scaling past $50M are especially vulnerable to confusing the two.

The insight that stops leaders cold: most organizations are not executing a bad sales strategy. They are executing no strategy at all, and calling it one.

Before you layer in AI or personalization, you need the foundation. Chapter 4 shows you what that actually looks like.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

post1.text:
Most growing companies treat branding as decoration. It is not. It is infrastructure.

Ulta Beauty's marketing approach proves this. Their CMO has built a system where brand identity and customer experience are not separate workstreams. They reinforce each other at every touchpoint. That is not a creative choice. That is an operational one.

For companies scaling past $50M, here is what this means in practice:

First, your brand is not your logo or your tagline. It is the experience your customer has every single time they interact with your company. What does that experience actually feel like? Second, omnichannel consistency is not a marketing problem. It is a leadership problem. If your sales team, your website, and your customer service are telling three different stories, you have an alignment failure at the top. Third, brand building and revenue generation are not in conflict. Companies that treat them as separate budgets are leaving compounding growth on the table.

The companies that scale fastest are the ones where the brand is felt internally before it is ever seen externally.

What does your brand actually smell like from the inside?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Fierce Pharma takes a close look at Eli Lilly's marketing culture and how it has evolved alongside the company's explosive growth. What stands out is not the budget or the campaigns. It is the internal culture that makes consistent, credible marketing possible at scale.

For companies in the $50M to $500M range, this is the part that usually gets skipped. Leaders invest in external marketing before they have built the internal culture that can support it. The result is messaging that does not hold up under scrutiny.

At Autobahn, we see this constantly. Brand credibility is built from the inside out. If your people do not believe the story, your customers will not either.

Read the full piece and ask yourself whether your marketing culture is ready for the growth you are chasing.

https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiqgFBVV95cUxObHJQeGMyVlVJNHF4NHlLZ2N5cldpRTY4ZnBYSUNFYmhkNlBJSkllY0Nwd0c1bnlOM0hTcklyOUlRcGRaLWYxWWQ0QUxjcER4TWVmQ01ZVjd4YUxjblZJN3BwSFBtWG9PTUUwRHBDMnRIVmVZTnlOMGRreVl6dlNtNkNlQXcydXI4NjZLNWttR0QweGlDcTJ6SzhUSmoxU1ZjVjFuVUpLU0djQQ?oc=5

post3.text:
Eli Lilly's marketing culture did not happen by accident. It was built intentionally, layer by layer, as the company scaled. That kind of deliberate brand-building is exactly what Chapter 5 of our upcoming book tackles head-on.

The chapter is called "What Does Your Marketing Smell Like?" and it was written by Kayli Simpson and Yasmin West. The title is provocative on purpose. Most executives can describe what their marketing looks like. Very few can describe what it feels like, or what signal it sends when no one is paying close attention.

Kayli and Yasmin work with scaling companies every day, and the pattern they see repeatedly is this: marketing breaks down between $50M and $500M not because of strategy, but because of identity. Leaders stop knowing what they stand for, and customers feel it.

Chapter 5 gives you a framework for fixing that before it costs you growth.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Your marketing budget is not your brand problem. Your clarity is. Companies scaling from $50M to $500M consistently hit a wall where their messaging fragments, their teams drift off-script, and their customers start getting mixed signals. The fix is not a new campaign. It is a hard look at what your brand actually communicates when no one is managing it.

post1.text:
Most companies scaling past $50M treat talent acquisition as a logistics problem. It is not. It is a strategic function, and the companies that figure that out first win.

Recent moves in the market tell the story clearly. Major enterprises are elevating talent acquisition leadership to global, executive-level roles. That is not a coincidence. It reflects a hard lesson scaling companies learn too late: who you hire to hire matters as much as who you hire.

Here is what that means in practice for leaders at $50M and beyond:

First, your talent function needs a seat at the strategy table, not just a slot in HR. Second, the profile of your talent leader should change as you scale. The person who worked at $20M cannot always build the engine you need at $200M. Third, referral networks and reactive recruiting will not sustain growth at this stage. You need proactive talent architecture.

The question is not whether your business is growing. The question is whether your talent function is growing with it.

What does your talent acquisition strategy look like at your current stage of growth?

post2.text:
A recent piece in CXO Digitalpulse covered Dana Duman stepping into a Vice President of Global Talent Acquisition role at Fortive, a multi-billion dollar industrial technology company.

Here is why that headline matters if you are running a $50M to $500M business.

Companies at scale are not just filling seats. They are building dedicated talent infrastructure with executive ownership. For mid-market leaders, that is the signal. If you are still treating talent acquisition as a task your HR generalist handles between other responsibilities, you are already behind the curve.

At Autobahn Consultants, we work with companies navigating exactly this inflection point. The shift from reactive hiring to a structured talent engine is one of the most critical and most underestimated moves a scaling company can make.

Read the full article here and ask yourself whether your talent function matches where your business is headed: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiowFBVV95cUxPMHlCV1Y4Xy0xZlVjR0NZdlB5VXpBNDhZOW0zeGduMTRTZzhSZXgyMHlVZ1Fpc1dETkhmUXlvWlBZcFplSmdZZlRIWWFSa2JBVHgwR0xqRDlHRFBIdWhhQi0zZWF5NHNLeTF6eW14azc2aW5sbGtBbXlORW1QQngzLUxSR2tHcVEyVi1qMlZDckRJd3huTFp0TGlwaTZvMVczZW5n?oc=5

post3.text:
The headlines keep confirming what we already know to be true for scaling companies: talent acquisition is a growth function, not an administrative one.

When Nucleus Software appointed a dedicated global head of talent acquisition, it was not a routine hire. It was a structural decision about how the company intends to scale.

Chapter 6 of Rock Your Business, titled The Talent Engine, addresses exactly this. Written by Caleb Hawkins, Darla Klein, and Yasmin West, the chapter unpacks why companies stall between $50M and $500M and how people strategy is almost always at the root of it.

One thing the authors make clear: building a talent engine requires intentional design. Most companies inherit a hiring process. The ones that scale well build one on purpose.

There is a difference, and it is significant.

post1.text:
More KPIs do not make better decisions. They make slower ones.

Most leadership teams above $50M have the opposite problem they think they have. They believe they lack visibility. In reality, they have too much noise and not enough signal. Oracle NetSuite recently catalogued 30 financial metrics companies might consider tracking. Thirty. For most scaling businesses, that list is a trap.

Here is what actually works at the $50M to $500M stage:

1. Fewer metrics, reviewed more often. A weekly look at five meaningful numbers beats a monthly review of fifty.

2. KPIs must connect directly to decisions. If a metric cannot change what you do next week, cut it.

3. Lagging indicators tell you what happened. Scaling companies need leading indicators that tell you what is about to happen.

The businesses that scale fastest are not the ones measuring everything. They are the ones who have agreed on what matters most and built discipline around those few things.

What is one metric your team tracks that nobody actually uses to make a decision?

post2.text:
A recent piece from CliftonLarsonAllen laid out the KPIs that help manufacturers improve company performance. Solid, practical content for any operations leader.

But here is the angle that matters most for scaling companies: knowing which KPIs to track is only half the problem. The harder question is who owns each metric, how often it is reviewed, and what action it is supposed to trigger.

At Autobahn, we see growing businesses drown in dashboards while starving for accountability. The right performance system connects your numbers directly to the people responsible for moving them.

If your team cannot tell you in 30 seconds what number they own and what they are doing about it this week, your KPI structure needs a rethink.

Read the CLA piece here and ask yourself which of these your team actually acts on: https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiugFBVV95cUxNc3hGVVVxVnMwVEpLcmxaNWJzaURJbERjczZaSDhlcnhvOFlHX1VZU0tETkctQjFqRVhZVkNtcFNoUWtfSmRhSmU5N3pYc25IVzlfTEs5TjFZWk1RTmhZd2JzSkpPSXVmQndRRHRBM29CaDBoWnVWRXcxMnBhWkcwT3dmWTAwSDFSeS1hYzFtRUNtd05nWE9PX25nbzRfc2ZzSjVFVURMY0hMRkdVMmtOdjVOYUluUXJIcEE

post3.text:
There is a chapter in our upcoming book that every leadership team tracking more than ten KPIs needs to read before their next planning meeting.

Chapter 7 of Rock Your Business is called Death by KPIs. Written by Hector Arias, Matt Radicelli, and Jim Randall, it tackles one of the most common traps we see in companies scaling from $50M and beyond: confusing activity with accountability.

The chapter does not tell you to track fewer things for the sake of simplicity. It gives you a specific way to evaluate whether each metric you are tracking is actually driving performance or just filling up a slide deck.

One question the authors ask will make your next leadership team meeting uncomfortable. In the best possible way.

Rock Your Business, available soon. Follow us for updates.

posts.blog_hook: Most leadership teams above $50M are not suffering from a lack of data. They are suffering from too much of it. When every department has a dashboard and every dashboard has 20 metrics, accountability disappears into the noise. The companies that scale fastest are not measuring more. They are measuring smarter, and they have built a culture where every number is owned by someone who acts on it.

post1.text:
Most companies are using AI wrong, and the results are proving it.

A recent Fortune survey found that nine out of ten executives say AI has not meaningfully improved productivity at their organizations. That is a staggering number, especially given the investment many of these companies have made.

Here is what scaling companies need to understand:

First, AI does not fix broken processes. It accelerates them, good or bad. If your operations are inefficient at $50M, adding AI tools makes the chaos faster.

Second, adoption without architecture fails. Buying tools is not a strategy. Leaders who win with AI define specific workflows before deploying technology inside them.

Third, the productivity gap is a people and change management problem as much as a technology problem. Your team needs a reason to use these tools and a structure that makes doing so the path of least resistance.

AI is not underperforming. Most implementations are.

If 90% of executives are not seeing results, what does your company need to change about how it is actually deploying these tools?

post2.text:
A recent piece in Fortune revealed that 90% of executives say AI has not boosted productivity at their companies. Even so, many are still moving forward with workforce reductions tied to AI adoption.

For companies in the $50M to $500M range, that sequence is a trap. The real opportunity is using AI to create leverage before you make structural decisions around people.

The most dangerous leader in a scaling company is not the one who doubts themselves. It is the one who stopped doubting themselves too soon.

Imposter syndrome gets treated like a problem to fix. But for leaders navigating the $50M to $500M growth stage, a calibrated sense of self-doubt is actually a competitive advantage. It keeps you asking better questions, listening to your team, and stress-testing your assumptions before the market does it for you.

Forbes Australia recently explored why high achievers continue to feel like frauds even at the top. The finding is worth sitting with: the feeling does not go away with more success. It scales with you.

Here is what that means in practice for leaders at your stage:

1. Stop trying to eliminate the doubt. Learn to operate alongside it.
2. The leaders who scale well are not the most confident ones. They are the most self-aware ones.
3. Psychological safety on your leadership team starts with you modeling honest uncertainty.

So here is the real question: Is your confidence building a stronger company, or just a more comfortable room?

A recent piece in Forbes Australia makes a point that every growth-stage executive should read: imposter syndrome does not shrink as you climb. It follows you up.

For companies scaling past $50M, this has a specific operational consequence. When senior leaders quietly doubt their own legitimacy, they over-index on control, under-delegate, and create bottlenecks that slow the entire organization down.

At Autobahn Consultants, we see this pattern constantly. The CEO who built the first $50M through sheer force of will often struggles to lead the next $450M because the skills that got them here are not the ones that get them there.

Recognizing imposter syndrome for what it is, a signal rather than a verdict, is one of the most practical leadership moves a scaling executive can make.

Read the full article and then ask yourself honestly: where is self-doubt quietly shaping your decisions right now?

post1.text:
Most $50M+ leaders have a detailed plan for scaling their business. Almost none have a plan for scaling their life.

That gap is where things fall apart.

Entrepreneur recently highlighted how founders pour years into building a company without ever asking what they actually want on the other side of it. That pattern does not stop at exit planning. It shows up every single day in how leaders structure their time, relationships, and energy.

Here is what high-growth leaders consistently miss:

First, revenue targets do not replace life targets. Hitting $200M means nothing if you have quietly sacrificed everything that made the journey worth it.

Second, work-life design is a leadership skill, not a perk. How you protect your capacity directly determines how well your organization performs.

Third, the leaders who scale furthest are not the ones who work the most hours. They are the ones who are intentional about which hours they give and to what.

The business will always demand more. The question is whether you have decided, in advance, what you are not willing to give it.

A recent piece in Fortune, in partnership with Morgan Stanley, lays out a roadmap for entrepreneurs navigating life after a business exit. It is worth reading for one reason most people miss: the emotional and identity disorientation that follows a sale is not a personal failure. It is a planning failure.

At Autobahn, we see this pattern long before an exit happens. Leaders who never defined what they were building toward, beyond the number, arrive at major milestones feeling hollow.

If you are scaling between $50M and $500M, now is the time to answer the question the transaction cannot answer for you: what does a great life actually look like, and are you building toward it?

Fortune and Morgan Stanley recently tackled what happens to entrepreneurs after a business exit. It is a conversation that starts too late for most leaders.

Chapter 10 of Rock Your Business, titled Coming Up for Air, takes that conversation and moves it much earlier in the journey. Co-authored by Samantha Frost and Jonathan and Katherine Slain, the chapter confronts a question most scaling leaders avoid: are you building a business that fits the life you actually want, or are you designing your life around a business that never stops asking for more?

One insight from the chapter that tends to stop leaders cold: coming up for air is not a reward you earn after hitting a milestone. It is a discipline you build before you need it.

There is a framework inside that changes how growth-stage leaders think about time, energy, and what they are ultimately building toward.
